title: Getting closer without arriving
objectives: Estimate a limit from a table and a graph
Tell a limit apart from the value of the function at that point

screens.prose: Take $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$. At $x = 1$ the top and the bottom are both 0, so the formula gives $\tfrac{0}{0}$, which is no number at all. The table tries inputs close to 1 instead.

state.caption: Top rows close in on 1 from below, bottom rows from above

screens.question: As $x$ closes in on 1 from both sides, what number do the outputs close in on?

widget.label: Number the outputs close in on
widget.accept: 2. The outputs run 1.9, 1.99, 1.999 from below and 2.1, 2.01, 2.001 from above.

hints.text: Read the $f(x)$ column from the top down to the middle row, then from the bottom up.
Each output sits close to the same whole number. How far off is 1.999? And 2.001?
From below: 1.9, 1.99, 1.999. From above: 2.1, 2.01, 2.001. Both sides squeeze in on one number.

feedback.correct: From both sides the outputs close in on 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ignore the middle row and watch where the outputs on either side of it are heading.

byKey.zero: You read $\tfrac{0}{0}$ as 0. It is no number at all, and the outputs near $x = 1$ are nowhere near 0.
byKey.input: 1 is the input we are closing in on. The question asks where the outputs, in the right-hand column, are heading.
byKey.last-row: 1.999 is the last row from below, not the end of the road. Closer inputs give 1.9999, then 1.99999, closing in on a round number.

explain.text: Above the middle row the outputs climb 1.9, 1.99, 1.999; below it they fall 2.1, 2.01, 2.001. Both sides close in on 2, though $f(1)$ itself does not exist. The formula fails at one point, yet the outputs around it still agree.

screens.prose: Here is the graph of the same $f$. It is a straight line with one point missing at $x = 1$: the open circle. Drag P along the curve.

derive.caption: P is at $x$ = {{fixed(P.x, 2)}}, height {{fixed(P.x + 1, 2)}}{{abs(P.x - 1) < 0.005 ? '. Exactly at 1 the formula gives 0/0' : ''}}

screens.question: Drag P towards the hole, first from the left, then from the right. Which statement fits what you see?

options.text: The height closes in on 2 from both sides, yet the curve has no point at $x = 1$
The height reaches 2 when P lands on $x = 1$
options.why: You expected the hole to fill in. At $x = 1$ the formula gives $\tfrac{0}{0}$, so the curve has no point there. The heights only close in on 2.

options.text: From the right the heights close in on a different number
options.why: You saw heights like 2.10 and 2.01 on the right. They are above 2, but they close in on 2 as well.

options.text: The heights shoot off near $x = 1$, as they do when you divide by 0
options.why: You treated the 0 on the bottom as the whole story. The top shrinks to 0 at the same time, and their ratio stays near 2.

hints.text: Watch the caption as P nears the open circle. What happens to the height?

feedback.correct: The heights close in on 2 from both sides, and $x = 1$ itself stays empty.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag P close to the hole from each side and read the height in the caption.

explain.text: At $x = 0.95$ the height is 1.95, and at $x = 1.05$ it is 2.05. Closer still gives 1.99 and 2.01, then 1.999 and 2.001. The heights head for 2, the height of the hole, from both sides.

canvas.caption: P at $x$ = 0.95, height 1.95. The hole sits at height 2

screens.prose: The number the outputs close in on is the **limit**. We write $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2$, read as the limit as $x$ tends to 1. Now try $g(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x} - 1}{x - 1}$, also $\tfrac{0}{0}$ at $x = 1$.

state.caption: Inputs closing in on 1 from below, then from above

screens.question: Estimate $\lim_{x \to 1} g(x)$.

widget.label: Estimate of the limit of g at 1

hints.text: Look at the two rows nearest the middle: 0.999 and 1.001.
0.500125 and 0.499875 sit either side of a simple number.
From below the outputs fall towards 0.5; from above they rise towards 0.5. The limit is 0.5.

feedback.correct: $\lim_{x \to 1} g(x) = 0.5$: the outputs squeeze in on it from both sides.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the number the two middle rows sit either side of.

byKey.zero: You read $\tfrac{0}{0}$ as 0 again. The outputs near 1 are all close to 0.5.
byKey.previous: 2 was the limit of $f$ on the last screens. This is a different function: read its own table.

explain.text: Above $x = 1$ the outputs are just under 0.5, and below it just over. Both sides close in on 0.5, so $\lim_{x \to 1} g(x) = 0.5$. A table gives a strong estimate; level 1's next lesson shows how to get it exactly.

screens.prose: Now only a graph. The curve of $h$ has a hole at $x = 2$: the function has no value there.
screens.question: What is $\lim_{x \to 2} h(x)$?

options.text: There is no limit, because $h(2)$ does not exist
options.why: You read the hole as the end of the story. The limit asks where the heights head as $x$ closes in on 2, and from both sides they head to 3.
2 is the input, on the $x$-axis. The limit is a height, read on the $y$-axis.
You read the empty hole as the value 0. An empty hole has no value at all, and the heights next to it are near 3.

hints.text: Put your finger on the curve left of the hole and slide it in. What height do you reach?
The open circle sits level with one of the grid lines.
From the left and from the right, the curve runs into the hole at height 3.

feedback.correct: The heights close in on 3 from both sides.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the curve into the hole from each side and read the height.

byKey.dne: You took the missing point as a missing limit. The limit never looks at $x = 2$ itself; it looks at the heights around it, which head to 3.

explain.text: Sliding in from either side, the curve heads for the hole at height 3. So $\lim_{x \to 2} h(x) = 3$, even though $h(2)$ does not exist. A hole is a missing value, not a missing limit.

canvas.caption: The limit is the height of the hole: 3

screens.prose: A new function $j$ jumps at $x = 0$. Closing in from the left only is written $x \to 0^-$; from the right only, $x \to 0^+$. The filled dot is $j(0)$.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: $\lim_{x \to 0^-} j(x) = 1$ and $\lim_{x \to 0^+} j(x) = 3$, so $\lim_{x \to 0} j(x)$ does not exist
$\lim_{x \to 0} j(x) = 3$, because $j(0) = 3$
options.why: You read the filled dot. It gives the value at 0, and the left side still heads to 1.

options.text: $\lim_{x \to 0} j(x) = 2$, half-way between
options.why: You averaged the two sides. No input near 0 gives a height near 2, so the heights are not heading there.

options.text: $\lim_{x \to 0} j(x) = 1$, because the left side comes first
options.why: You closed in from the left only. A limit needs both sides to agree, and the right side heads to 3.

hints.text: Follow the left piece in to $x = 0$, then the right piece.
The left piece ends at an open circle. Read its height.
From the left the heights head to 1; from the right, to 3. Two different numbers cannot both be the limit.

feedback.correct: The one-sided limits are 1 and 3. They disagree, so there is no limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the height each side heads to, then compare them.

byKey.value: You let the filled dot decide. $j(0) = 3$ is the value at 0; the left side still heads to 1, so the sides disagree.

explain.text: From the left the heights head to 1, and from the right to 3. These are the one-sided limits. A limit exists only when they agree, so $\lim_{x \to 0} j(x)$ does not exist.

canvas.caption: Left side heads to 1, right side to 3: no limit

screens.prose: An edge case: $s(x) = \sin(1/x)$ near $x = 0$. Run A uses $x = \tfrac{1}{2\pi k}$ and Run B uses $x = \tfrac{1}{2\pi k + \pi/2}$. Both runs close in on 0 as the whole number $k$ grows.

state.caption: Run A outputs: 0, 0, 0, ... Run B outputs: 1, 1, 1, ...

screens.question: Does $\lim_{x \to 0} \sin(1/x)$ exist?

options.text: No: two runs closing in on 0 give outputs stuck at 0 and stuck at 1, so no single number fits
Yes, it is 0: Run A shows it
options.why: You trusted one run of inputs. Run B closes in on 0 just as well, and its outputs stay at 1.

options.text: Yes, it is 0.5, between the runs
options.why: You averaged the runs. Other runs give −1, or 0.3, or anything in between: the outputs never settle.

options.text: No, because $s(0)$ is not defined
options.why: That is not the reason. $f$ was undefined at 1 and still had a limit. Here the outputs refuse to settle.

hints.text: Compare the two $s(x)$ columns. Are they heading to the same number?
Run A's dots all sit at height 0 and Run B's at height 1.
Near 0, $1/x$ races through every angle, so the outputs swing between −1 and 1 forever. No number is closed in on.

feedback.correct: The outputs swing between −1 and 1 however close you get, so there is no limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A limit needs every run of inputs closing in on 0 to give outputs closing in on the same number.

byKey.zero: You stopped at Run A. Run B also closes in on 0, but its outputs stay at 1, so 0 cannot be the limit.

explain.text: As $x$ shrinks, $1/x$ grows through every multiple of $2\pi$, so the curve swings faster and faster. Run A lands on the zeros and Run B on the peaks. Outputs that never settle mean no limit, even without a hole or a jump.

screens.prose: Someone set $k(2) = 1$ by hand. The filled dot is that value. The curve itself has a hole at $x = 2$.
screens.question: What is $\lim_{x \to 2} k(x)$?

options.why: You read the filled dot. That is $k(2)$, the value at 2. The limit uses only inputs near 2, never 2 itself.

options.text: It does not exist
options.why: You took the hole as a missing limit. Both sides still close in on 4; a dot sitting elsewhere does not change that.
2 is the input. The limit is a height.

The curve runs into the open circle from both sides.
Inputs like 1.99 and 2.01 give heights near 4. The dot at height 1 is only what happens at 2 exactly.

byKey.value: You took the limit to be the value of the function there. The value $k(2) = 1$ is a single dot; the heights around it all head to 4.

explain.text: Near $x = 2$ the heights head for the open circle at 4, from both sides. So $\lim_{x \to 2} k(x) = 4$, while $k(2) = 1$. The limit and the value are different questions, and here they have different answers.

screens.prose: Each time you ignored $x = a$ and watched the heights nearby. $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$$ means $f(x)$ gets as close to $L$ as we like once $x$ is close enough to $a$, from both sides, with $x \neq a$. If the one-sided limits differ, there is no limit.

Changing the single value $f(2)$

explain.text: The definition looks at inputs close to $a$ but never equal to it. So the value $f(2)$ and anything far from 2 are irrelevant. Only the curve right beside $x = 2$ matters.

screens.prose: Why did the first table's outputs miss 2 by exactly the gap between $x$ and 1? Put $x = 1 + h$ with $h \neq 0$: $$f(1 + h) = \frac{(1 + h)^2 - 1}{h} = \frac{2h + h^2}{h}$$
screens.question: Simplify $f(1 + h)$ for $h \neq 0$.

hints.text: Divide each term on top by $h$.
$\dfrac{2h}{h} = 2$ and $\dfrac{h^2}{h} = h$.

feedback.correct: $f(1 + h) = 2 + h$: the output sits exactly $h$ away from 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide both terms of $2h + h^2$ by $h$.

byKey.early: You set $h = 0$ in the second term. That gives the limit, but $f(1 + h)$ itself still carries an $h$.
byKey.no-divide: That is the top only. Divide it by $h$.
byKey.form: That is equal, but not simplified. Cancel the $h$ from each term on top.

explain.text: $f(1 + h) = 2 + h$, so the output is exactly $h$ away from 2. At $h = -0.01$ it is 1.99, and at $h = 0.001$ it is 2.001. As $h \to 0$ the gap shrinks to nothing, which is why the limit is 2.

screens.prose: As more market makers quote a stock, its spread $s$ shrinks. The bid always sits a quarter of the spread below a fair price $p$, and the ask three quarters above.
screens.question: As the spread shrinks to 0, what price do the bid and the ask both close in on?

widget.label: Price both quotes close in on
widget.accept: £100.12: the bid plus a quarter of the spread, on every row.

hints.text: The bid is $p$ minus a quarter of the spread. Use any row to find $p$.
Take the first row: bid £100.02, spread £0.40.

feedback.correct: Both quotes close in on £100.12 as $s \to 0^+$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the quarter-spread offset on the bid to find the price both quotes head for.

byKey.last-mid: £100.13 is the latest midpoint. It sits a quarter of the spread above $p$, so it is still heading down, to £100.12.
byKey.first-mid: £100.22 is the midpoint at the widest spread. The quotes keep moving as the spread shrinks.
byKey.last-bid: £100.11 is the latest bid. It is still a penny below where the bid is heading.

explain.text: The bid is $p - \tfrac{s}{4}$ and the ask $p + \tfrac{3s}{4}$, so both close in on $p = \text{£}100.12$ as $s \to 0$. A spread cannot be negative, so this is a one-sided limit, $s \to 0^+$. The midpoint, $p + \tfrac{s}{4}$, heads there too, but from above.

ideas: A limit is the number the outputs close in on as the input closes in on $a$, from both sides.
The limit ignores $x = a$ itself: a hole or a misplaced dot there does not change it.
If the one-sided limits differ, or the outputs never settle, there is no limit.

formula.name: Limit
formula.tex: \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \iff \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L
formula.note: $x$ gets close to $a$ but never equals it.

You took the right side only. The left side heads to 2.
